questions.q: Why is catching `except ValueError` specifically usually better than a bare `except:` when processing CSV rows?
options: A bare except: would also silently swallow unrelated bugs, like a typo causing a KeyError, instead of letting them surface
ValueError is the only exception type Python actually supports
Bare except: blocks are a syntax error in Python
There is no difference between them
questions.explain: Catching a specific exception type lets genuinely different problems still surface loudly, instead of all being swallowed the same way.

questions.q: In orders.csv, why doesn't int(row["quantity"]) raise an exception on order 1014, even though its quantity (-1) is a real data-entry error?
options: "-1" parses fine as a valid integer — it's logically wrong, not a type error, so you have to raise the exception yourself
int() always raises an exception on negative numbers
Order 1014 doesn't actually exist in the dataset
csv.DictReader automatically removes negative values
questions.explain: Python happily parses "-1" as an integer; catching the business-rule violation requires an explicit raise in your own validation code.

questions.q: When does the `else` block attached to a try statement run?
options: Only if the try block completed with no exception raised
Only if an exception was raised and caught
Always, regardless of whether an exception occurred
Only if the except block is missing entirely
questions.explain: else on a try/except is the "it succeeded" branch — it never runs if an exception was raised.

questions.q: What is the defining characteristic of a finally block?
options: It runs whether or not an exception occurred, making it the right place for cleanup that must always happen
It only runs if no exception was raised
It replaces the need for a try block entirely
It can only contain a single line of code
questions.explain: finally runs unconditionally — exception or not — which is why connection/file-closing code belongs there.

questions.q: In this lesson's row-processing lab over orders.csv, how many of the 20 rows should end up skipped?
options: 2 — the blank customer_name row and the negative quantity row
0 — orders.csv has no data issues
20 — every row fails
5 — one per data column
questions.explain: Orders 1005 (blank customer_name) and 1014 (negative quantity) are the two rows a correct version of this script skips.
